notes.heading: Simple Linear Regression and Gauss-Markov Assumptions

bullets.text: OLS estimates minimize the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)², yielding the slope estimate b₁ = Cov(x, y) / Var(x).
Under assumptions MLR.1–MLR.5, OLS is BLUE: the best linear unbiased estimator.
Unbiasedness requires assumptions MLR.1–4. Adding homoskedasticity (MLR.5) is required for efficiency.

notes.heading: Multiple Regression and Omitted Variable Bias

bullets.text: β₁ measures the partial effect of x₁ on y holding x₂ fixed, reflecting a ceteris paribus interpretation.
Omitting a relevant variable that is correlated with x₁ causes b₁ to be biased, with Bias(b̃₁) = β₂ · δ̃₁.
Heteroskedasticity means the conditional variance of the error depends on the regressors: Var(uᵢ | xᵢ) = σᵢ².
Under heteroskedasticity, OLS remains unbiased, but standard errors are biased, rendering standard t and F tests invalid. Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors fix this.
Autocorrelation occurs when errors in different periods are correlated, such as AR(1) errors uₜ = ρuₜ₋₁ + eₜ, invalidating standard errors.

flashcards.front: What does the slope estimate b₁ represent mathematically in simple linear regression?
What conditions are required for OLS to be BLUE?
What is the formula for omitted variable bias when a relevant variable x₂ is omitted?
flashcards.back: Bias(b̃₁) = β₂ · δ̃₁, where δ̃₁ is the slope from regressing x₂ on x₁.

flashcards.front: How many dummy variables should be included in a regression for g groups when an intercept is present?
flashcards.back: g − 1 dummies to avoid the dummy variable trap (perfect collinearity).

flashcards.front: What happens to OLS estimates and standard errors in the presence of heteroskedasticity?
flashcards.back: Estimates remain unbiased and consistent, but the usual standard errors are biased.

flashcards.front: What does a Durbin–Watson statistic value near 2 indicate?

quiz.prompt: What happens to the OLS estimator if the assumption of homoskedasticity (MLR.5) is violated?
options: OLS becomes biased and inconsistent.
OLS remains unbiased, but the usual standard errors are biased.
OLS loses its unbiased property but gains maximum efficiency.
OLS becomes invalid and cannot be computed.
quiz.explanation: Heteroskedasticity does not affect the unbiasedness or consistency of OLS coefficients, but it makes the standard error formulas incorrect, invalidating standard hypothesis tests.
quiz.explain_reason: Slide 7 explicitly summarizes that OLS estimates are still unbiased and consistent under heteroskedasticity, but standard errors are biased.

quiz.prompt: If you omit a relevant variable x₂ from a regression model, when will the coefficient b₁ for x₁ remain unbiased?
options: When x₂ has zero variance.
When x₁ and x₂ are uncorrelated, making the auxiliary regression slope δ̃₁ equal to zero.
When the sample size n is extremely large.
When heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are used.
quiz.explanation: The omitted variable bias is given by β₂ · δ̃₁. If x₁ and x₂ are uncorrelated, δ̃₁ = 0, so the bias disappears.
quiz.explain_reason: Slide 11 shows that the bias depends on the regression slope of x₂ on x₁, demonstrating that uncorrelated variables cause no omitted variable bias.

quiz.prompt: Why must you include g − 1 dummy variables instead of g dummies when modeling g distinct groups with an intercept?
options: Including all g dummies creates perfect collinearity, known as the dummy variable trap.
Including g dummies would violate the assumption of homoskedasticity.
Including g dummies causes the residuals to sum to a positive number.
Including g dummies makes the error term autocorrelated.
quiz.explanation: Including a dummy for every single group alongside an intercept leads to perfect multicollinearity, making it impossible to compute OLS.
quiz.explain_passage: Slide — the dummy variable trap — slide 6
quiz.explain_reason: Slide 6 explicitly states that including all g dummies creates perfect collinearity.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary purpose of using heteroskedasticity-robust (White) standard errors?
options: To make OLS estimates more efficient than WLS.
To eliminate the bias in OLS coefficient estimates caused by heteroskedasticity.
To provide valid t statistics and confidence intervals in large samples even when errors are heteroskedastic.
To test whether the error term is normally distributed.
quiz.explanation: Robust standard errors do not change the coefficient estimates; they correct the standard errors so that inference remains valid in the presence of heteroskedasticity.
quiz.explain_reason: Page 3 notes that robust t statistics are valid in large samples whether or not errors are homoskedastic.

quiz.prompt: What does a Durbin–Watson statistic value significantly different from 2 suggest about a time series model?
options: The model suffers from heteroskedasticity.
There is presence of first-order autocorrelation in the error terms.
The regressors are perfectly collinear.
The model is misspecified due to an omitted variable.
quiz.explanation: The Durbin-Watson d statistic approximates 2(1 − ρ̂), so values near 2 imply no autocorrelation, while values far from 2 indicate autocorrelation.
quiz.explain_passage: ECON301 Lecture 8 — Time series and autocorrelation.pdf — page 11
quiz.explain_reason: Page 11 links the Durbin-Watson statistic directly to ρ̂ and indicates that values near 2 mean no first-order autocorrelation.

quiz.prompt: What differentiates the Gauss-Markov assumptions required for unbiasedness from those required for BLUE?
options: MLR.1 through MLR.4 ensure unbiasedness, while adding MLR.5 (homoskedasticity) achieves BLUE status.
MLR.5 ensures unbiasedness, while MLR.1 through MLR.4 ensure efficiency.
Unbiasedness requires homoskedasticity, whereas BLUE only requires linearity.
There is no difference; all Gauss-Markov assumptions are required solely for unbiasedness.
quiz.explanation: Unbiasedness only needs assumptions MLR.1 to MLR.4. Homoskedasticity (MLR.5) is needed on top of that to make OLS the best linear unbiased estimator.
quiz.explain_passage: My notes: when is OLS BLUE? — paragraph 1
quiz.explain_reason: Your notes clearly state that unbiasedness needs MLR.1-4, and BLUE additionally needs homoskedasticity (MLR.5).
